concept: Human adoption of LLM vocabulary and its effect on tic baselines
summary: Source-anchored research for Human adoption of LLM vocabulary and its effect on tic baselines. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: A preregistered experiment (496 participants) found brief chatbot interaction makes participants adopt specific words, persisting through distractor tasks, supporting exposure-to-active-vocabulary as the mechanism. (low confidence)

Corpus check on the International Corpus of English found no evidence that focal words like delve are especially prevalent in any English variety, contradicting the Nigerian-English/RLHF-rater-origin explanation; RLHF itself remains a candidate cause. (medium confidence)

A preregistered experiment (496 participants) showed brief chatbot interaction made people adopt its vocabulary, giving a causal mechanism beyond correlational baseline comparisons. (medium confidence)
Enriching TOEFL essay vocabulary with ChatGPT cut the false positive rate from 61.22% to 11.77%, showing detectors key on vocabulary and predictability, not authorship. (medium confidence)

LLM-marker usage varies widely: about 20% in computational fields and in China/South Korea/Taiwan, about 5% in English-speaking countries; MDPI (21%) and Frontiers (20%) exceed Nature/Science (~7-10%). Measured rates are likely lower bounds. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-07-01)

Sourati et al. (USC) report declining writing-complexity variance on Reddit, news and academic preprints, and that LLM polishing/rewriting reduces that variance (reported 21-50% across datasets/models); the review cites this as evidence of stylistic homogenization in scientific writing. (medium confidence)

Even when prompted for grammar-only edits, LLMs substantially alter meaning; in a user study heavy LLM use raised neutral-stance essays by nearly 70%, and AI-generated peer reviews scored about one point higher than expected and devalued clarity and significance. (low confidence)

Marker words are not stable baselines: per search summaries of the Yakura paper (v3), delve later declined below its pre-ChatGPT baseline in some categories (Science & Tech -15%, Education -11%, Business -30%), so a static pre-LLM frequency list can mislead. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)

Model collapse under a replace-data regime (each generation's synthetic data replaces the prior data) degrades models, but if synthetic data accumulate alongside the original real data, test error has a finite upper bound independent of iteration count; this held across language models, diffusion models and VAEs. (medium confidence)

The excess-word method cannot flag individual abstracts, cannot separate direct LLM use from stylistic borrowing, and cannot fully separate LLM effects from other emerging linguistic trends. (low confidence)

Seven GPT detectors misclassified non-native English TOEFL essays as AI with 61.22% average false positive rate, versus 5.19% on US 8th-grade essays; the mechanism is perplexity, since lower lexical variability reads as machine-like. (high confidence)

Excess-vocabulary analysis found 454 excess style words in 2024 biomedical abstracts, versus 190 at the 2021 COVID peak; the authors estimate at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts were LLM-processed. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-07-01)

Cited evidence that people adopt LLM framing (Jakesch et al. 2023) and that AI-assisted ideation reduces semantic diversity (Anderson et al. 2024) supports the mechanism, but the review notes longitudinal effects and correlation-versus-causation gaps remain open. (low confidence)

Rewriting experiments apply one LLM uniformly to all abstracts, so they give an upper bound on homogenization rather than real-world practice; effects are stronger for Reddit and academic writing than for news. (low confidence)

Florida State University (Juzek et al.) analysed 22.1 million words of science/tech conversational podcasts; nearly three-quarters of target AI buzzwords rose after ChatGPT, some more than doubling. 'Underscore' rose while its synonym 'accentuate' did not, which points to AI-specific rather than generic drift. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2025-08-26)

Kobak et al. measure LLM vocabulary influence as excess word frequency in 15M+ PubMed abstracts (2010-2024) versus pre-LLM years, an approach modelled on excess-mortality studies; they report a lower bound of at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts LLM-processed, up to 40% in some subcorpora. (high confidence)

Yakura et al. use a synthetic-control method on 737,083 hours of podcast speech (824,634 episodes) plus YouTube academic talks: treated words like delve are compared with a weighted mix of donor words sharing pre-ChatGPT trends, and show an abrupt post-release rise. (high confidence)

Wikipedia's Signs of AI writing guide says its signs indicate potential problems, not proof, that it is not a ban on words, and that treating signs as problems to fix could make detection harder. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)
Tic vocabulary shifts by model generation (earlier delve/intricate, newer enhance/showcase), so a fixed word list decays and needs dating. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)

A 2026 arXiv paper reports that writing style (vocabulary complexity, formality) is a confound causing detector false positives on academic writing, so formal human prose can be flagged. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-08-28)
The Nigerian-English explanation for 'delve' is contested: comparing base Llama 2 to its RLHF-tuned version suggests RLHF preference itself promotes such words. (low confidence)

A Max Planck study of 737,083 hours of podcast speech (824,634 episodes) found abrupt post-ChatGPT increases in words such as delve, showcase, boast, intricacies and meticulous; synthetic-control analysis supports a causal link, and the authors frame it as machines trained on human data feeding their traits back into human language. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-07-16)
A preregistered experiment (N=496) found brief chatbot interaction led participants to adopt the chatbot's words, persisting through a distractor task and in forced lexical choice. (low confidence)

The term 'model collapse' is used inconsistently in the literature and is conflated with generic performance loss or any synthetic-data training; critics argue claims of inevitable collapse need scoping to the specific definition and data regime. (low confidence)

Yakura et al. (Max Planck) analysed about 737,083 hours of unscripted conversation from 824,634 podcast episodes and report that ChatGPT-favoured words (delve, showcase, boast, meticulous) rose abruptly in spontaneous speech after ChatGPT's release; they use synthetic-control analysis to argue for a causal link. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-07-16)

The 'GPT words' list was derived by having ChatGPT edit millions of emails, essays and articles and extracting words it repeatedly added; usage was then tracked in about 360,000 YouTube academic talks and 771,000 podcast episodes, with a surge within roughly 18 months of release. (medium confidence)
The measured effect is lexical only; the Max Planck paper does not test semantic or grammatical influence and frames vocabulary as an early indicator of wider cultural influence. (medium confidence)

Juzek and Ward take PubMed 2020 as the pre-LLM reference (LLMs not widespread before 2021), compare it with 2024, and define 21 focal words by three criteria: significant 2020-2024 rise, unexplained spike, and ChatGPT overuse relative to human abstracts. (medium confidence)
